name: Virginia Woolf
summary: English modernist writer whose political essays treat patriarchy as the root of militarism and dictatorship and argue that women, barred from the institutions of power, should stay outside patriotic and martial loyalties. A Room of One's Own and Three Guineas press for women's access to education and the professions and reject pride of nationality, fascism and dictatorship; in 1940 she nonetheless wrote that a woman who believes the English fight protects freedom must support it as far as she can.

notes: Woolf was a novelist and essayist, not a politician, and her political writing is concentrated in A Room of One's Own, Three Guineas and a few late essays, so most statements are null. Themes searched: war and pacifism, patriotism and nation, empire, fascism and dictatorship, education, the professions, property and women's money, religion and the Church, class and the working class, press and honours. Three Guineas proposes a state wage for marriage and motherhood and a Society of Outsiders; these match no statement closely and were left null (the outsiders' refusal of arms-making is a personal stance, not a call to abolish armed forces). On the fighting instinct she writes that the outsider 'cannot judge' it and leaves men free to deal with it, so war-builds-character is null. Her diaries contain antisemitic remarks; they are words about people, not positions on any statement, and her published writing condemns persecution of Jews. Economic, healthcare, trade, environment and many government statements have no stated position in the texts read. Library and web searches for further open full texts (Labour Party involvement, suffrage work) found only catalogue pages and a blocked journal (403), which was not retried.
